finding.claim: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user record via Object.assign and persists it, letting a user set any model field (e.g. role, isAdmin, orgId, email, id) that should be server-owned.
finding.source: req.body (attacker-controlled JSON) in the PUT /me handler
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5 followed by req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6

trace.note: Object.assign copies every own key of req.body onto req.user with no allow-list
req.store.save persists the modified user record

finding.guards_checked: No allow-list, schema validation, or field filtering in users.js. Auth middleware that sets req.user and store-level write restrictions are not in the repo and could not be checked. Impact depends on the user model's fields, which were not provided.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js: no allow-list, schema validation, or field filtering between req.body and req.store.save. The auth middleware that sets req.user and any store-level write restrictions are not in the repo (Glob shows only users.js).
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (users.js:4-7: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at line 5 is followed by req.store.save at line 6 with no filtering), but the repo does not show whether /me is behind authentication (req.user is never set here), what fields the user model has (so whether role/isAdmin/orgId exist to escalate with), or whether req.store.save enforces write restrictions, so impact and attacker reachability cannot be decided from this code.
